glossary.definition: The negatively charged particle found in every atom, carrying −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. In copper about one electron per atom is free to move through the whole lattice, and these free electrons carry the current.

drills.prompt: What is the charge of one electron?

choices.feedback: That is the proton's charge. The electron's is the same size but negative.
A coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons; one electron carries only −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
9.109 × 10⁻³¹ is the electron's mass in kilograms, not its charge.

drills.prompt: A copper wire carries 1 A. What moves along the wire to carry the current?

choices.text: Free electrons drifting through the lattice

choices.feedback: The copper ions are fixed in the lattice; they vibrate in place but don't travel. Moving ions carry current in an electrolyte, not in a metal.

choices.text: Protons, in the direction of conventional current
choices.feedback: Protons stay in the nuclei and never move along a wire. Conventional current is a sign convention, not a description of what moves.

drills.prompt: Which statement about the free electrons in a wire is true?

choices.text: They drift opposite to the conventional current arrow.
They drift in the direction of the conventional current arrow.
choices.feedback: Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so they drift the other way.

choices.text: The battery supplies them, and the load uses them up.
choices.feedback: The electrons were already in the wire, about one per atom in copper. The battery pushes them around the loop and gets back as many as it sends out; the load converts their energy, not the electrons.

drills.prompt: About how many electrons pass a point each second in a current of 1 A?

choices.feedback: That is the charge of one electron, in coulombs. The count is 1 C/s divided by it: 1 / (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 6.24 × 10¹⁸ per second.
That is Avogadro's number, the atoms in a mole. A coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
An ampere is one coulomb per second, and a coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

glossary.definition: An atom or molecule with more or fewer electrons than protons, so it carries a net charge. In an electrolyte, including the one inside a cell, ions rather than free electrons carry the current.

drills.prompt: Inside a cell, what carries the current through the electrolyte between the two electrodes?

choices.feedback: An electrolyte has almost no free electrons; the current crosses it as moving ions. Electrons carry it only in the electrodes and the outside wires.
Holes are a semiconductor's carriers. In an electrolyte the carriers are ions.

drills.prompt: What makes an atom an ion?

choices.text: It has gained or lost electrons, so its charges no longer balance.
It has gained or lost protons.
choices.feedback: Changing the number of protons changes the element itself, a nuclear process. Chemistry moves electrons.

choices.text: It is moving through a liquid.
choices.feedback: Motion doesn't change charge: a neutral molecule moving through water is not an ion.

choices.text: It has more neutrons than protons.
choices.feedback: Neutrons carry no charge, so they make a different isotope, not an ion.

drills.prompt: A neutral sodium atom loses one electron. What is the charge of the ion?

choices.feedback: Losing a negative electron leaves one more proton than electrons, so the ion is positive.
The atom was neutral; taking away −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C leaves +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
One elementary charge is 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; a coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ of them.

drills.prompt: Salt water conducts well and distilled water barely does. Why?

choices.text: The dissolved salt splits into ions that are free to move.
The salt adds free electrons to the water.
choices.feedback: Dissolved salt adds Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not free electrons; the ions carry the current.

choices.text: The salt lowers the water's breakdown voltage.
choices.feedback: Conducting at a few volts needs mobile charge carriers, not breakdown. The salt supplies them as ions.

glossary.definition: A liquid, paste, gel or solid that conducts by the movement of ions, not free electrons. It carries the current between the electrodes inside a cell, and in an aluminum electrolytic capacitor it makes contact with the oxide dielectric.

drills.prompt: Which of these conducts by moving ions rather than free electrons?

choices.text: The paste inside an alkaline cell

choices.feedback: Copper conducts by free electrons, about one per atom.
Silicon conducts by electrons and holes; its atoms stay fixed in the crystal.
Graphite conducts by electrons moving within its carbon layers.

drills.prompt: Which is true of an aluminum electrolytic capacitor?

choices.text: It is polarized: reversed voltage damages its oxide layer.

choices.feedback: The electrolyte conducts; it serves as the negative plate, in contact with the oxide. The dielectric is the thin aluminum oxide on the positive foil.

choices.text: It can be connected either way around.
choices.feedback: Its oxide dielectric is formed for one polarity. Reversed, the oxide breaks down, leakage current rises, and the capacitor can overheat or vent.

drills.prompt: Why does a cell's internal resistance rise when it gets cold?

choices.text: Ions move more slowly through the colder electrolyte.
The free electrons in its leads slow down.
choices.feedback: Metal leads conduct slightly better when cold. The rise comes from the electrolyte, where the ions move more slowly.
The EMF is set by the chemistry and changes little with temperature. The internal resistance is a separate thing, set largely by the electrolyte.

glossary.definition: The property of particles that makes them exert electric forces on each other, measured in coulombs (C). It is conserved: a circuit moves charge around a loop and never uses it up, and charging a capacitor moves charge from one plate to the other through the circuit, leaving the capacitor's total charge zero.

drills.prompt: Which unit measures electric charge?

choices.feedback: The ampere measures current, the rate of flow of charge: 1 A = 1 C/s.
The volt measures energy per unit charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
The farad measures capacitance, charge per volt: 1 F = 1 C/V.

drills.prompt: A current of 2 A flows for 3 s. How much charge passes a point?

choices.feedback: Charge is current times time, Q = I·t = 2 A × 3 s = 6 C, not t/I.
That is I/t. Charge is current times time: Q = I·t = 6 C.
Joules measure energy. Charge is in coulombs: Q = I·t = 6 C.

drills.prompt: A cell is "dead". What has it run out of?

choices.text: The chemical energy that does work on the charge

choices.feedback: Charge is conserved: a cell moves charge around the loop and gets it all back. A dead cell has used up its reactants, the stored chemical energy.
Current is a rate of flow, not something stored. What a cell stores is chemical energy.

drills.prompt: A capacitor is charged to 5 V. What is the total charge on it, both plates together?

choices.text: Zero: +Q on one plate and −Q on the other
Q = CV, all on the positive plate
choices.feedback: Charging moves Q from one plate to the other through the circuit, so one plate holds +Q and the other −Q. "The charge on a capacitor" means Q on each plate, not a net charge.
The source pumps no net charge into the capacitor; it moves charge from one plate to the other, leaving +Q and −Q, a total of zero.

glossary.definition: The rate at which charge passes a point, I = Q/t, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s). Schematics draw conventional current, the direction positive charge would move, opposite to the electrons' drift in a metal.

drills.prompt: 1 A is the same as:

choices.feedback: A joule per second is a watt, a rate of energy. Current is a rate of charge: 1 A = 1 C/s.
A joule per coulomb is a volt. 1 A = 1 C/s.
Volts per second measures how fast a voltage changes, as in a slew rate. 1 A = 1 C/s.

drills.prompt: A lamp is in series with a battery. Compare the current into the lamp with the current out of it.

choices.text: Less comes out, because the lamp uses some of it.
choices.feedback: Charge doesn't pile up in the lamp, so as much current leaves as enters. What the lamp uses is energy: the charge leaves it at a lower potential.

choices.text: It depends on which way the electrons drift.
choices.feedback: Whichever way the carriers move, the current is the same at both terminals of a two-terminal part; only the sign convention depends on direction.

drills.prompt: Which measurement needs the meter in series, breaking the circuit to insert it?

choices.feedback: A voltmeter goes across two points, in parallel; a voltage belongs to two points.
An ohmmeter goes across a part with the circuit unpowered; it doesn't go in series with a live loop.

drills.prompt: Which relation defines current?

choices.feedback: Q·t grows with time; current is charge per unit time, I = Q/t.
That is Ohm's law, a property of a resistance. Current itself is the rate of charge flow, I = Q/t, in any part.
From P = V·I, I = P/V, not P·V; and the definition is I = Q/t.

glossary.definition: The energy each coulomb gains or gives up between two points, V = W/Q, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). A voltage always belongs to two points; a node voltage is measured from ground.

drills.prompt: 1 V is the same as:

choices.feedback: A coulomb per second is an ampere. A volt is energy per charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
A joule per second is a watt. 1 V = 1 J/C.

drills.prompt: A meter shows "the voltage at node B" as 3.3 V. What does that mean?

choices.text: Node B is 3.3 V above ground.

choices.feedback: Voltage doesn't flow; current does. A voltage is between two points, here node B and ground.

choices.text: Node B holds 3.3 V of charge.
choices.feedback: Charge is measured in coulombs. A node voltage is the potential difference from ground to node B.

drills.prompt: 2 C of charge gains 18 J passing through a source. What is the voltage across the source?

choices.feedback: V = W/Q = 18 J / 2 C = 9 V, not W·Q.
That is Q/W. Voltage is energy per charge: V = W/Q = 9 V.
18 J is the energy for all 2 C; each coulomb gains 9 J, so V = 9 V.

drills.prompt: Two points are joined by a wire of negligible resistance carrying 2 A. What is the voltage between them?

choices.feedback: V = I·R with R ≈ 0 gives about 0 V, whatever the current.

choices.text: It can't be known without the source voltage
choices.feedback: The source voltage drops across the other parts; across a near-zero resistance V = I·R ≈ 0.

glossary.definition: Electromotive force: the work a source does on each coulomb passing through it, from its chemistry or from a changing magnetic field, in volts. A source's terminal voltage equals its EMF only when no current flows.

drills.prompt: In what unit is EMF measured?

choices.feedback: Despite its name, EMF is not a force: it is work per unit charge, joules per coulomb, which is volts.
EMF is energy per charge, in volts; the current it drives depends on the rest of the circuit.
EMF is energy per coulomb (volts), not energy per second (watts).

drills.prompt: A cell has an EMF of 1.5 V and an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω, and delivers 0.4 A. What is its terminal voltage?

choices.feedback: That is the EMF, what it reads with no current. With 0.4 A flowing, 0.4 A × 0.5 Ω = 0.2 V drops inside, leaving 1.3 V.
While the cell delivers current the internal drop subtracts: V = E − I·r = 1.3 V. It adds only while the cell is being charged.
0.2 V is the drop inside the cell; the terminals show what's left: 1.5 − 0.2 = 1.3 V.

drills.prompt: When does a voltmeter across a cell read its EMF?

choices.text: When no current flows from the cell

choices.feedback: Shorted, the terminal voltage is near zero: the whole EMF drops across the internal resistance.

choices.text: When it delivers its rated current
choices.feedback: Delivering current, it loses I·r inside, so the terminals read less than the EMF.

drills.prompt: Which of these produces an EMF?

choices.text: A coil whose magnetic flux is changing

choices.feedback: A resistor has a voltage across it, but it takes energy from the charge (V = I·R); it doesn't do work on it. An EMF does work on the charge.

choices.text: A wire at rest in a steady magnetic field
choices.feedback: A steady field through a stationary loop induces nothing; an EMF needs the flux through the loop to change.

glossary.definition: The resistance inside a source, from its electrolyte, electrodes and contacts (or a generator's or transformer's windings). A current I drops I·r inside the source, so the terminal voltage is E − I·r.

drills.prompt: A battery reads 9.0 V with no load and 8.0 V while delivering 0.5 A. What is its internal resistance?

choices.feedback: 9 V / 0.5 A is the resistance of the whole loop. Only the 1 V drop happens inside: r = 1 V / 0.5 A = 2 Ω.
8 V / 0.5 A = 16 Ω is the load. The internal drop is 9.0 − 8.0 = 1 V, so r = 1 V / 0.5 A = 2 Ω.
r = ΔV/I = 1 V / 0.5 A = 2 Ω, not I/ΔV.

drills.prompt: A shorted car battery can deliver hundreds of amperes; a shorted AA cell only a few. Mainly why?

choices.text: The car battery's internal resistance is far lower.
The car battery's EMF is higher.
choices.feedback: 12 V against 1.5 V is a factor of 8, but the short-circuit currents differ by far more. I = E/r is set mostly by r: milliohms for a car battery, a fraction of an ohm for an AA cell.

choices.text: The car battery stores more energy.
choices.feedback: Capacity sets how long it lasts, not how much current it can push at once; the short-circuit current is E/r.

drills.prompt: A cell's voltage sags when a load is connected and recovers when it's removed. What explains this?

choices.text: The load current drops I·r across the internal resistance.
The EMF falls while current flows.
choices.feedback: The EMF is set by the chemistry and stays nearly the same; the drop is I·r inside the cell, and it goes away when the current stops.

choices.text: The wires to the load lose charge.
choices.feedback: Wires don't lose charge. The terminal voltage falls by I·r, the drop across the internal resistance.

glossary.definition: The voltage across a part divided by the current through it, R = V/I, in ohms. For a wire or a film it is set by the material's resistivity, the length and the cross-section: R = ρL/A.

drills.prompt: Which is the same as 1 Ω?

choices.feedback: A/V is the siemens, the unit of conductance, the reciprocal of resistance.
V·A is the unit of power (a watt for DC). Resistance is volts per ampere.
Ω·m is resistivity, a property of the material. A part's resistance is in ohms, V/A.

drills.prompt: A wire is replaced by one of the same metal, twice as long and with twice the cross-sectional area. Its resistance:

choices.feedback: Twice the length doubles R, but twice the area halves it: R = ρL/A is unchanged.
Length and area act in opposite directions in R = ρL/A: 2/2 = 1, so R is unchanged.
Twice the area halves R, but twice the length doubles it: R = ρL/A is unchanged.

drills.prompt: You double the voltage across a 1 kΩ resistor. What happens?

choices.text: The current doubles; the resistance stays 1 kΩ.
The resistance doubles and the current stays the same.
choices.feedback: Resistance is a property of the part (its material and shape), not of the voltage applied. For a resistor, I = V/R doubles.
Current is proportional to voltage, I = V/R. It's the power that quadruples, P = V²/R.

drills.prompt: Which has the higher resistance when lit: a 60 W, 120 V lamp or a 100 W, 120 V lamp?

choices.feedback: At a fixed voltage P = V²/R, so more power means less resistance: 240 Ω for 60 W against 144 Ω for 100 W.
Same voltage, different power: R = V²/P gives 240 Ω and 144 Ω.

glossary.definition: A property of a material, ρ in Ω·m: the resistance of a piece 1 m long with a cross-section of 1 m². Copper's is about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C, and in a metal it rises with temperature.

drills.prompt: Resistivity is measured in:

choices.feedback: Ohms measure a piece's resistance, which depends on its shape. Resistivity belongs to the material: Ω·m.
Ω/m is the resistance per length of one particular wire, which depends on its cross-section. From R = ρL/A, ρ = R·A/L, in Ω·m.
S/m is conductivity, the reciprocal of resistivity.

drills.prompt: You cut a copper wire in half. What changes for each half?

choices.text: Its resistance halves; its resistivity is unchanged.

choices.feedback: Resistivity belongs to the material, copper, not to the piece. Only the resistance, R = ρL/A, halves with the length.

choices.text: Nothing: resistance is a property of copper.
choices.feedback: That describes resistivity. Resistance depends on the length too: R = ρL/A halves.

drills.prompt: As a copper wire warms up, its resistivity:

choices.feedback: In a metal the lattice vibrates harder when hot and scatters the free electrons more, so resistivity rises, about 0.4 % per °C for copper. Falling with temperature is typical of semiconductors.

choices.text: stays the same: resistivity is a constant
choices.feedback: It is a property of the material at a given temperature; copper's rises about 0.4 % per °C.

drills.prompt: A piece of material has resistance R, length L and cross-sectional area A. Its resistivity is:

choices.feedback: From R = ρL/A, solve for ρ: multiply by A and divide by L, ρ = R·A/L.
V/I is the resistance of this one piece. Resistivity takes the shape out: ρ = R·A/L.

glossary.definition: A material with many free charge carriers, so a small voltage drives a large current; in copper, about one free electron per atom. A wire on a schematic stands for a conductor whose resistance is negligible.

drills.prompt: Which conducts best at room temperature?

choices.feedback: Pure silicon is a semiconductor, far more resistive than copper; doping helps but comes nowhere near a metal.
Pure water has very few ions, so it conducts poorly; tap water and salt water conduct because of their dissolved ions.
Glass is an insulator: its electrons are held in their atoms and bonds.

drills.prompt: What does a wire drawn on a schematic mean?

choices.text: A connection whose resistance is small enough to ignore: both ends are one node.
A connection with exactly zero resistance in the real circuit.
choices.feedback: Real wires and traces have some resistance; the schematic assumes it is negligible. Where it matters (long runs, large currents), it is drawn as a resistor.

choices.text: A path along which the voltage drops gradually.
choices.feedback: A schematic wire is ideal: both ends are at one voltage. Any drop that matters is drawn as a part.

drills.prompt: Why does a metal conduct so well?

choices.text: About one electron per atom is free to move through the lattice.
Its positive ions move toward the negative terminal.
choices.feedback: A metal's ions are fixed in the lattice; only the free electrons move through it.

choices.text: Its electrons are bound tightly to their atoms.
choices.feedback: That describes an insulator. In a metal, about one electron per atom is free.

glossary.definition: A material with almost no free charge carriers, such as glass, PVC or air, because its electrons are held in their atoms and bonds. Its current is negligible until the field is strong enough to break it down.

drills.prompt: Which of these is an insulator?

choices.feedback: Aluminum is a metal, a good conductor.
Salt water conducts through its dissolved ions.
Graphite conducts by electrons moving within its carbon layers.

drills.prompt: Which is true of an insulator?

choices.text: A strong enough field breaks it down and makes it conduct.
It conducts no current at any voltage.
choices.feedback: Every insulator breaks down above its dielectric strength (dry air at roughly 3 kV/mm), and a tiny leakage current flows even below it.
Its atoms have as many electrons as any other material's; they are bound to their atoms and bonds, not free to move.

drills.prompt: Why does glass insulate?

choices.text: Almost none of its electrons are free to move.

choices.feedback: Glass is full of charge, electrons and nuclei; it is neutral overall, and the charges are not free to move.

choices.text: Its electrons drift too fast to be steered.
choices.feedback: Drift is the slow net motion of free carriers; glass has almost no free carriers to drift at all.

glossary.definition: A material such as silicon whose conductivity lies between a conductor's and an insulator's and is set mainly by doping: a trace of another element supplies free electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type). Diodes and transistors are made from it.

drills.prompt: What makes n-type silicon different from pure silicon?

choices.text: A trace of a donor element such as phosphorus supplies free electrons.
It carries a net negative charge.
choices.feedback: Doped silicon is neutral: each free electron is balanced by a fixed positive donor ion. The "n" names the majority carrier, not a net charge.

choices.text: Its atoms are packed more densely.
choices.feedback: Doping replaces only a tiny fraction of the atoms; the crystal is the same, but the number of free carriers rises enormously.

drills.prompt: As pure silicon warms up, its resistance:

choices.feedback: In a metal the number of carriers is fixed and they scatter more when hot. In a semiconductor heat frees many more carriers, so resistance falls.
Heat frees more carriers in a semiconductor, so its resistance falls steeply.

drills.prompt: In p-type silicon, the majority carriers are:

choices.text: positive ions moving through the crystal
choices.feedback: The acceptor ions are fixed in the crystal. What moves are holes: missing electrons in the bonds, which act as positive carriers.
Those are the minority carriers in p-type silicon; acceptors create holes.
Protons never leave the nuclei. A hole is a missing electron in the bonds that behaves like a positive carrier.

drills.prompt: Which part is made from doped semiconductor?

choices.feedback: Carbon film is a resistive film with no junction; it is not a doped semiconductor device.
Aluminum foil, oxide and electrolyte: no semiconductor.

glossary.definition: The slow average velocity of the charge carriers along a conductor, v = I/(nAe), typically well under a millimeter per second in a copper wire. It is a small net motion on top of a fast random one that averages to zero.

drills.prompt: You flip a switch and a lamp 3 m away lights at once. Why, if the electrons drift so slowly?

choices.text: The field travels along the wire close to light speed and sets the electrons everywhere moving at once.
Electrons from the switch race to the lamp close to light speed.
choices.feedback: Each electron drifts well under 1 mm/s. The wire is already full of free electrons, and the field reaches all of them almost at once.

choices.text: The lamp lights only once electrons from the switch reach it.
choices.feedback: At under 1 mm/s that would take most of an hour or more. The lamp lights because the electrons already in its filament start moving when the field arrives. On AC they never arrive at all; they only oscillate in place.

drills.prompt: The same current flows in a wire with twice the cross-sectional area. The drift velocity:

choices.feedback: v = I/(nAe): the same current spread over twice the area needs each carrier to move only half as fast.
v = I/(nAe) depends on A: twice the area, half the drift velocity.

drills.prompt: Roughly how fast do electrons drift in a 1 mm² copper wire carrying 3 A?

choices.feedback: That is how fast the field, the signal, travels along the wire, not the electrons. v = I/(nAe) ≈ 0.2 mm/s here.
That is the electrons' random speed in copper, which averages to zero. The net drift for 3 A in 1 mm² is about 0.2 mm/s.

glossary.definition: The rate of energy transfer, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). For any two-terminal part P = V·I; in a resistance this is P = I²R = V²/R.

drills.prompt: 1 W is the same as:

choices.feedback: A joule is energy; a watt is energy per second.
A volt per ampere is an ohm. For DC, 1 W = 1 V·A = 1 J/s.
A kilowatt-hour is energy (3.6 MJ): power multiplied by time.

drills.prompt: The current through a resistor doubles. Its power:

choices.feedback: P = I²R: power goes with the square of the current, so twice the current gives four times the power.
P = I²R rises with current; twice the current gives four times the power.

drills.prompt: A 12 V motor draws 2 A; a 24 V heater draws 1 A. Which takes more power?

choices.text: The motor, because it draws more current.
choices.feedback: P = V·I: 12 V × 2 A = 24 W and 24 V × 1 A = 24 W.

choices.text: The heater, because its voltage is higher.
choices.feedback: P = V·I: 24 V × 1 A = 24 W, the same as 12 V × 2 A.

drills.prompt: P = I²R and P = V²/R apply to:

choices.text: a resistance, where V = I·R holds
any two-terminal part, such as an LED or a motor
choices.feedback: Those forms assume V = I·R. For any part P = V·I; an LED or a motor has no fixed V/I.
They hold at each instant in AC too, and with RMS values they give the average power in a resistor.

glossary.definition: Power turned into heat in a part, such as I²R in a resistor. The part warms until heat escapes as fast as it is made; its power rating is the dissipation that brings it to its highest safe temperature at a stated ambient temperature, derated above that.

drills.prompt: A ¼ W resistor dissipates 0.4 W. What happens?

choices.text: It runs hotter than it is rated for and may drift, discolor or fail.
It limits its power to ¼ W by raising its resistance.
choices.feedback: A resistor doesn't regulate its power; it dissipates V²/R whatever its rating, and the excess shows up as temperature.

choices.text: Nothing: ratings leave a large safety margin.
choices.feedback: The rating is the dissipation that takes it to its highest safe temperature at the stated ambient; above it the part overheats.

drills.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor has 5 V across it. How much power does it dissipate?

choices.feedback: 5 V / 100 Ω = 0.05 A is the current. P = V²/R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W.
That is V·R. P = V²/R = 0.25 W.
P = V²/R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W; check the decimal point.

drills.prompt: A resistor is rated for its full power up to 70 °C ambient. Inside an enclosure at 100 °C, it can safely dissipate:

choices.feedback: The rating brings it to its highest safe temperature from a 70 °C ambient. Starting hotter, less dissipation reaches that limit, so it is derated.

choices.text: more than its rating, since it is already warm
choices.feedback: A warmer start leaves less room before its temperature limit, so it can dissipate less, not more.

glossary.definition: The charge a capacitor holds per volt across it, C = Q/V, in farads. For parallel plates C = ε·A/d: larger plates, a thinner gap and a dielectric of higher permittivity all raise it.

drills.prompt: 1 F is the same as:

choices.feedback: Capacitance is charge per volt, C = Q/V, so 1 F = 1 C/V.
A volt-second per ampere is a henry, the unit of inductance. A farad is 1 C/V.
A joule per coulomb is a volt.

drills.prompt: The gap between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor is halved. Its capacitance:

choices.feedback: C = εA/d: a thinner gap gives more capacitance, not less.
C goes as 1/d, not 1/d²: half the gap, twice the capacitance.

drills.prompt: A 10 µF capacitor holds 50 µC. What is the voltage across it?

choices.feedback: V = Q/C = 50 µC / 10 µF = 5 V; the micro prefixes cancel.
That is C/Q. V = Q/C = 5 V.

drills.prompt: Two equal capacitors in parallel give:

choices.feedback: In parallel the plate areas add, so the capacitances add: 2C. Half is what two in series give.
In parallel both store charge at the same voltage, so the charges add: 2C.

glossary.definition: The insulator between a capacitor's plates. Its permittivity, with the plate area and gap, sets how much charge the capacitor holds per volt, and the field it can stand before breaking down limits the capacitor's voltage rating.

drills.prompt: In a ceramic capacitor, the dielectric is:

choices.text: the ceramic layer between the electrodes

choices.feedback: The electrodes are conductors; the dielectric is the insulator between them.
The leads only connect the electrodes to the circuit.

drills.prompt: The air between two plates is replaced by a dielectric with four times the permittivity. The capacitance:

choices.feedback: C = εA/d: a higher permittivity gives more capacitance.

choices.text: stays the same, since the plates and gap are unchanged
choices.feedback: C depends on the material between the plates too: C = εA/d.

drills.prompt: What sets a capacitor's voltage rating?

choices.text: The field its dielectric can stand before it breaks down

choices.feedback: Area sets the capacitance. The rating is set by the field in the dielectric, about V/d, against its breakdown strength.

choices.text: The capacitance: larger capacitors take higher voltages
choices.feedback: There is no such rule. For a given dielectric, a thicker layer raises the rating and lowers the capacitance.

drills.prompt: To raise a capacitor's voltage rating with the same dielectric material, you can:

choices.text: make the dielectric thicker, and accept less capacitance

choices.feedback: Larger plates raise the capacitance but not the field, V/d, which sets breakdown.
A thinner layer raises the field V/d at a given voltage, so it breaks down sooner.

glossary.definition: The magnetic flux linkage per ampere of a coil, L, in henries; it sets the voltage a changing current induces, v = L·di/dt. It grows with the square of the number of turns and with the core's permeability.

drills.prompt: 1 H is the same as:

choices.feedback: A coulomb per volt is a farad.

drills.prompt: A coil's turns are doubled on the same core. Its inductance:

choices.feedback: Inductance goes with the square of the turns: twice the turns makes twice the flux, linked by twice the turns.

choices.feedback: v = L·di/dt, and a steady current has di/dt = 0, so v = 0. L·I is the flux linkage (20 mWb), not a voltage.

drills.prompt: The current in a 1 mH inductor rises at 1000 A/s. The voltage across it is:

choices.feedback: v = L·di/dt = 0.001 H × 1000 A/s = 1 V; the millihenry matters.

glossary.definition: A voltage induced in a coil by changing magnetic flux, in the direction that opposes the change producing it. In an inductor it is L·di/dt and opposes any change of current (Lenz's law); in a turning motor it is generated by the rotation, grows with speed and opposes the supply, so a stalled motor has none and draws its largest current.

drills.prompt: When does a DC motor draw the most current?

choices.text: At standstill: stalled or just starting
At full speed with no load
choices.feedback: At speed the back-EMF nearly cancels the supply, so little current flows. At standstill there is no back-EMF, and only the winding resistance limits the current.

drills.prompt: In a turning DC motor, the back-EMF is proportional to:

The current sets the torque. The back-EMF is generated by the rotation, in proportion to the speed.

glossary.definition: A set of points joined by wire, all at one voltage. Each terminal of a part connects to exactly one node, and the currents into a node sum to zero (Kirchhoff's current law).

drills.prompt: Wires join one end of a resistor, one end of a capacitor and a transistor's emitter, with no part between them. These points form:

choices.feedback: An open passes no current at all.

a third of the supply across each

page.definition: The time that sets how fast a first-order circuit settles: τ = RC for a resistor and capacitor, τ = L/R for an inductor and resistor. After one τ a step response has covered 63.2 % of the way to its final value; after 5τ it is within 1 % (99.3 %).
page.physics:
While a capacitor charges through R from a step of V_S, the current is set by the voltage still left across R: i = (V_S − v_C)/R. That current is the rate the capacitor charges, C·dv_C/dt. So the closer v_C gets to V_S, the slower it moves, and the gap still to close shrinks by the same fraction in every equal slice of time: v_C(t) = V_S(1 − exp(−t/τ)). Each τ leaves e⁻¹ ≈ 36.8 % of the gap there was at its start.

An inductor does the same with current. Its voltage is v_L = L·di/dt, and as the current through R rises, less of the supply is left across the inductor, so the current rises more slowly: i(t) = (V_S/R)(1 − exp(−t/τ)) with τ = L/R. On either curve, the starting slope carried straight on would reach the final value at exactly t = τ.
page.units: Ohms times farads is seconds: 1 Ω × 1 F = (1 V/A)(1 A·s/V) = 1 s. Henries over ohms is seconds too: 1 H = 1 V·s/A, so 1 H / 1 Ω = 1 s. On a breadboard τ runs from under a nanosecond (a 50 Ω source driving 10 pF gives 500 ps) to seconds (10 kΩ with 100 µF gives 1 s).

confusions.title: τ is not 1/f_c.
confusions.text: 1/(RC) is the corner in radians per second; in hertz the cutoff is f_c = 1/(2πRC). For 1 kΩ and 100 nF, τ = 100 µs and f_c ≈ 1.59 kHz, not 10 kHz.

confusions.title: 63 %, not 37 %.
confusions.text: After one τ a charging capacitor has covered 63.2 % (1 − e⁻¹) of the step; e⁻¹ ≈ 36.8 % is the part still to go. A discharging capacitor is at 36.8 % of where it started.

confusions.title: Not "full after one τ".
confusions.text: An exponential never quite arrives. Engineers call it settled after 5τ (99.3 %); an input that must settle to half a step of a 12-bit converter (1 part in 8192) needs about 9τ.

confusions.title: The R is the one the capacitor sees.
confusions.text: A source resistance R_s in front of R adds to it: τ = (R_s + R)C. Fed from a divider, the capacitor charges through R1∥R2 plus any series R. Find it by setting the sources to zero and looking back from the capacitor's terminals.

glossary.definition: The frequency at which a filter's output has fallen to 1/√2, about 70.7 %, of its passband value: down 3 dB. For a first-order RC filter it is 1/(2πRC), where the capacitor's reactance equals the resistance.

drills.prompt: An RC low-pass uses R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 100 nF. What is its cutoff frequency?

choices.feedback: 1/(RC) = 10 000 is in radians per second. Divide by 2π for hertz: 1/(2π × 1.0 kΩ × 100 nF) ≈ 1.6 kHz.
RC = 100 µs is the time constant, a time. The cutoff frequency is 1/(2πRC) ≈ 1.6 kHz.
That is 2π/(RC); the 2π belongs with RC in the denominator: f_c = 1/(2πRC) ≈ 1.6 kHz.

drills.prompt: A sine at exactly the cutoff frequency passes through an RC low-pass. The output is:

choices.text: about 70.7 % of the input amplitude, lagging it by 45°
zero, since the cutoff is where the filter stops passing signal
choices.feedback: A first-order filter rolls off gradually: down 3 dB at f_c, then 20 dB per decade. Nothing is cut off sharply there.
Half the power, not half the voltage: −3 dB is 1/√2 of the voltage, about 70.7 %.

drills.prompt: You double the capacitor in an RC low-pass. The cutoff frequency:

choices.feedback: More capacitance means less reactance at each frequency, so X_C comes down to R at half the frequency: 1/(2πRC) halves.

choices.text: stays the same, because R sets it
choices.feedback: Both R and C set it: f_c = 1/(2πRC), so doubling C halves f_c.

page.unit: hertz (Hz); in radians per second, ω_c = 2πf_c
page.definition: The frequency at which a filter's output has fallen to 1/√2 ≈ 70.7 % of its passband level: 3 dB down, half the power into the same load. For a first-order RC filter f_c = 1/(2πRC); for an RL filter f_c = R/(2πL).
page.physics:
In an RC low-pass, the capacitor's reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls as the frequency rises, so the capacitor takes a smaller share of the input. R and C form a divider, but their voltages are 90° apart, so they add like the sides of a right triangle: |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/f_c)²). At f_c, X_C equals R: the two voltages are the same size, the output is 1/√2 of the input, and it lags the input by 45°.

Well above f_c, |H| ≈ f_c/f: the output halves for every doubling of frequency, −6 dB per octave or −20 dB per decade. Well below f_c the output follows the input with almost no loss and little phase shift.
page.units: Hertz, cycles per second. Datasheets and Bode plots give hertz; the algebra often uses ω in rad/s (ω = 2πf), and mixing the two is an error of 2π, about 6.3×. Audio filters sit between about 20 Hz and 20 kHz; the filter in front of an ADC sits below half its sample rate; an RC that smooths a low-current analog supply pin (100 Ω, 1000 µF) sits near 1.6 Hz.

confusions.title: Not where the signal stops.
confusions.text: At f_c the output is still 70.7 % of the input. A first-order filter rolls off gently: one decade above f_c it still passes about 10 % (−20 dB).

confusions.title: −3 dB is half the power, not half the voltage.
confusions.text: Half the voltage is −6 dB. At f_c the voltage ratio is 0.707; into the same load resistance power goes as V², so the power ratio is 0.5.

confusions.title: Hertz, not radians per second.
confusions.text: 1/(RC) is ω_c in rad/s. For 1 kΩ and 100 nF, 1/(RC) = 10 000 rad/s, but f_c = 1.59 kHz.

confusions.title: The source and the load move it.
confusions.text: A source resistance adds to R and lowers f_c. A load resistance R_L across the capacitor lowers the passband gain and leaves the capacitor charging through R∥R_L, so the corner 3 dB below the new passband rises. Measured against the input instead, the output falls to 70.7 % of it at a lower frequency, or never, if the load already costs more than 3 dB.

A scope's or amplifier's rated bandwidth is its −3 dB frequency.

glossary.definition: A logarithmic measure of a ratio: 10·log₁₀ of a power ratio, or 20·log₁₀ of a voltage ratio when both voltages are across equal resistances. The 20 comes from power going as voltage squared, so a change gives the same number of decibels whether you measure its power or its voltage.

drills.prompt: An amplifier's voltage gain is 100. What is that in decibels?

choices.feedback: 10·log₁₀(100) = 20 is the power formula. For a voltage ratio use 20·log₁₀: 20 × 2 = 40 dB.
Decibels are logarithmic: each factor of 10 in voltage adds 20 dB, so 100 = 10² is 40 dB.
log₁₀(100) = 2 is only the logarithm. Multiply by 20 for a voltage ratio: 40 dB.

drills.prompt: A filter attenuates a signal by 20 dB. By what factor did its voltage fall?

choices.feedback: 100 is the power ratio for 20 dB. The voltage ratio is 10^(20/20) = 10; power goes as voltage squared, so 10² = 100.
Decibels aren't a ratio themselves. Voltage ratio = 10^(dB/20) = 10.

drills.prompt: Two amplifier stages in cascade have gains of 20 dB and 6 dB. What is the total gain?

choices.feedback: Gains multiply, and logarithms turn products into sums, so decibels add: 20 + 6 = 26 dB. That is about 20 times in voltage (10 × 2).
Both stages amplify, so their decibels add: 20 + 6 = 26 dB, a voltage ratio of about 10 × 2 = 20.

glossary.definition: The opposition a capacitor or inductor offers to alternating current, in ohms: X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls with frequency, and X_L = 2πfL rises with it. A reactance stores energy and returns it each cycle instead of dissipating it, so its current is 90° out of phase with its voltage.

drills.prompt: In what unit is reactance measured?

choices.feedback: Farads measure capacitance, a property of the part. Reactance is the ratio of AC voltage to AC current, so it is in ohms, like resistance.
Reactance depends on frequency, but it is a ratio of voltage to current: ohms.

drills.prompt: What is the reactance of a 1.0 µF capacitor at 1.0 kHz?

choices.feedback: That is 2πfC itself, 6.3 mS, a conductance-like quantity. Reactance is its reciprocal: 1/(2π × 1000 Hz × 1.0 µF) ≈ 159 Ω.
1/(f·C) = 1.0 kΩ leaves out the 2π: X_C = 1/(2πfC) ≈ 159 Ω.
That is the reactance of 0.1 µF, a slip of ten in the capacitance. With 1.0 µF: 1/(2π × 1000 Hz × 1.0 µF) ≈ 159 Ω.

drills.prompt: A capacitor and an inductor each sit across a sine source. The frequency is raised tenfold at the same amplitude. Their currents:

choices.text: the capacitor's rises tenfold and the inductor's falls tenfold

choices.feedback: Only the capacitor's: X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls as f rises, but X_L = 2πfL rises, so the inductor's current falls.

choices.text: neither changes, since only resistance limits current
choices.feedback: Reactance limits AC current too, and it depends on frequency: X_C falls tenfold, X_L rises tenfold.

drills.prompt: An ideal capacitor carries 10 mA RMS with 5 V RMS across it. What average power does it dissipate?

choices.feedback: V·I gives the average power only when voltage and current are in phase. In a capacitor they are 90° apart: it takes energy in one quarter-cycle and returns it in the next.
There is no factor of a half that applies here: voltage and current are 90° apart, so the average power is zero.

glossary.definition: The total opposition of a circuit to alternating current, combining resistance and reactance; its magnitude |Z| is the ratio of AC voltage to AC current, in ohms. Resistance and reactance are 90° apart, so in series they combine like the sides of a right triangle: |Z| = √(R² + X²).

drills.prompt: A 30 Ω resistor is in series with a reactance of 40 Ω. What is the magnitude of the impedance?

choices.feedback: Adding them directly treats R and X as in phase. They are 90° apart, so |Z| = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω.
Reactance doesn't subtract from resistance; they combine at right angles: √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω.

drills.prompt: A series RC is driven at the frequency where X_C equals R = 1.0 kΩ. What is |Z|?

choices.feedback: R and X_C are 90° apart and don't add directly: |Z| = √(1.0² + 1.0²) kΩ ≈ 1.41 kΩ.
An inductor's and a capacitor's reactances can cancel; a resistance and a reactance can't. They combine at right angles: about 1.41 kΩ.
The reactance adds to the resistance at right angles, so |Z| is more than R: √2 × 1.0 kΩ ≈ 1.41 kΩ.

drills.prompt: Which is true of impedance?

choices.text: Its magnitude can change with frequency, because it includes reactance.
It is another name for resistance.
choices.feedback: Resistance dissipates and doesn't depend on frequency. Impedance also includes reactance, which stores energy and changes with frequency.

choices.text: A series RC has less impedance than its resistance alone.
choices.feedback: The reactance combines with R at right angles: |Z| = √(R² + X²) is never less than R.

page.definition: The ratio of a sinusoidal voltage to the current it drives, counting both size and phase. It is written as a complex number Z = R + jX: the resistance R dissipates power, the reactance X stores energy and returns it. Its magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²) is the ratio V_rms/I_rms you would measure.
page.physics:
A resistor's current is in phase with its voltage. A capacitor's current is largest where its voltage crosses zero (changing fastest, i = C·dv/dt) and zero at the voltage peaks, so it leads the voltage by 90°. An inductor's voltage is largest where its current changes fastest (v = L·di/dt), so its current lags by 90°. In series the same current flows through every part, so their voltages add with their phases: 3 V across R and 4 V across C give 5 V across both, not 7 V.

Impedance packs this into one number per part. In series, impedances add: Z = R + j(X_L − X_C) (X_C as a positive size, so a capacitor's X is −X_C), with X_L = 2πfL and X_C = 1/(2πfC). In parallel, their reciprocals (admittances) add. Since X depends on frequency, so does Z: a series RC looks like the capacitor at low frequencies and like the resistor at high ones.
page.units: Ohms, volts per amp, like resistance. The phase angle φ = atan(X/R), the angle by which the voltage leads the current, runs from −90° (pure capacitance) through 0° (pure resistance) to +90° (pure inductance). Loudspeakers are rated 4 Ω or 8 Ω nominal; RF cables and instruments are built for 50 Ω; a scope input is 1 MΩ in parallel with about 15 pF.

confusions.title: Not R + X as plain numbers.
confusions.text: 1 kΩ in series with a capacitor whose reactance is 1 kΩ gives |Z| = 1.41 kΩ, not 2 kΩ: the two voltages are 90° apart.

confusions.title: Impedance is not reactance.
confusions.text: Reactance X is only the part from capacitance and inductance; impedance includes resistance too. A plain resistor has an impedance and no reactance.

confusions.title: An ohmmeter doesn't measure it.
confusions.text: A multimeter's ohms range measures with DC: it reads a capacitor as open once the meter's test current has charged it (a large one shows the reading climbing first), and an inductor as its winding resistance. Impedance needs an AC test signal at the frequency of interest, from an LCR meter, or from V and I measured together.
