glossary.definition: How far one sine wave is shifted in time from another of the same frequency, given as an angle in which a full period is 360°. A capacitor's current leads its voltage by 90°, an inductor's lags by 90°, and a resistor's is in phase.

drills.prompt: Two 1 kHz sine waves reach their peaks 0.25 ms apart. What is the phase difference?

choices.feedback: Time must be converted to a fraction of the period. At 1 kHz the period is 1 ms, and 0.25 ms is a quarter of it: 90°.
At 1 kHz a period is 1 ms, so 0.25 ms is a quarter period, 360°/4 = 90°.
The period at 1 kHz is 1 ms; 0.25 ms is 25 % of it, and 25 % of 360° is 90°.

drills.prompt: An ideal capacitor is driven by a sine voltage. Its current:

choices.text: peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage does

choices.feedback: That is a resistor. A capacitor's current is C·dv/dt, largest where the voltage changes fastest, at the zero crossings, a quarter cycle before the voltage peak.

choices.text: peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage does
choices.feedback: That is an inductor, whose voltage is L·di/dt. A capacitor's current leads its voltage.

drills.prompt: An inverting amplifier with a gain of −2 amplifies a low-frequency sine. The output's phase relative to the input:

choices.text: 180°: it peaks when the input is at its lowest

choices.feedback: The amplifier multiplies by a negative number at every instant, which turns the wave upside down: 180°. A quarter-cycle shift needs a reactance.
A positive gain wouldn't. The minus sign flips the wave, a 180° shift.

glossary.definition: A circuit that passes frequencies below its cutoff and attenuates those above it. The simplest is a series resistor followed by a capacitor to ground: at high frequencies the capacitor's falling reactance shunts the signal away from the output.

drills.prompt: Which arrangement is an RC low-pass filter?

choices.text: A resistor in series from input to output, and a capacitor from the output to ground
A capacitor in series from input to output, and a resistor from the output to ground
choices.feedback: That is a high-pass: the series capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies.

choices.text: A capacitor straight across the source, with nothing in series
choices.feedback: With no series resistance an ideal source simply drives the capacitor: the output equals the input at every frequency. The filter needs R to take the high-frequency part of the signal.

drills.prompt: A first-order low-pass has its cutoff at 1 kHz. About how much of a 10 kHz sine gets through?

choices.text: About a tenth of it (−20 dB)
None of it, since it is above the cutoff
choices.feedback: A first-order filter rolls off at 20 dB per decade. One decade above f_c the gain is about f_c/f = 0.1, not zero.
That is the gain at f_c itself. At ten times f_c it is about f_c/f = 0.1.

drills.prompt: A 5 V square wave at 20 kHz drives an RC low-pass whose time constant is 100 times the period. The output is:

choices.text: a nearly steady level at the wave's average, with a small ripple
a copy of the square wave
choices.feedback: The square wave's fundamental is far above the cutoff, so the filter strips it and its harmonics; only the average, the DC part, passes.

choices.text: 0 V, since the filter blocks the 20 kHz signal
choices.feedback: It blocks the switching, not the average. DC sits below every cutoff, so the average level passes unchanged.

glossary.definition: An integrated differential amplifier whose output is a very large open-loop gain, often 100 000 or more, times the difference between its two inputs. That gain is too large and too variable to use directly, so circuits set their gain with negative feedback through resistors.

drills.prompt: An op amp with negative feedback works in its linear range. Which is true?

choices.text: The output moves until the two inputs are at almost the same voltage.
Its two inputs are joined inside the chip.
choices.feedback: Nothing inside joins them, and they draw almost no current. Their equal voltages are the result of feedback, which is why the rule fails without it.

choices.text: Its inputs draw whatever current the circuit needs.
choices.feedback: An ideal op amp's inputs draw no current; real ones draw picoamps to nanoamps.

drills.prompt: An op amp on ±12 V supplies has no feedback, an open-loop gain of 200 000, V+ = 2.010 V and V− = 2.000 V (ignore input offset). Its output sits:

choices.text: near the positive rail, a little below +12 V

choices.feedback: 10 mV × 200 000 asks for 2000 V, but the output can't go beyond its supplies; it stops near +12 V.
10 mV is the input difference. With no feedback, the whole open-loop gain multiplies it.

choices.text: at 0 V, since the inputs are almost equal
choices.feedback: The inputs are held equal only by negative feedback. Without it, 10 mV of difference drives the output to a rail.

drills.prompt: A voltage follower ties an op amp's output to its − input and feeds the signal to its + input. Why is V_out = V_in?

choices.text: Feedback drives the output until V− equals V+, and V− is the output itself.

choices.feedback: Its open-loop gain is huge. Feedback sets the closed-loop gain to 1.

choices.text: The input is wired straight through to the output.
choices.feedback: The output comes from the supplies through the op amp's output stage. That is why a follower can drive a load the signal source couldn't.

glossary.definition: Returning part of an amplifier's output so that it subtracts from the input, which makes any error at the output partly cancel itself. With enough open-loop gain, the closed-loop gain is set by the feedback network, usually resistors, rather than by the amplifier.

drills.prompt: Which connection gives an op amp negative feedback?

choices.text: A resistor from the output to the inverting (−) input
A resistor from the output to the non-inverting (+) input
choices.feedback: That is positive feedback: a rise at the output raises V+, which pushes the output further up. It makes a Schmitt trigger, not an amplifier.

choices.text: A resistor from the output to ground
choices.feedback: That is a load; nothing returns to an input.

drills.prompt: A non-inverting stage with resistors for a gain of 10 is built with op amps whose open-loop gain ranges from 100 000 to 300 000. The stage's gain:

choices.text: is within about 0.01 % of 10 for all of them
ranges over a factor of three, like the op amps
choices.feedback: Feedback makes the gain about 1/β = 10; the open-loop gain A only sets the small error: 10/(1 + 10/A) = 9.999 at A = 100 000.
That is the open-loop gain, with no feedback. The resistors set the closed-loop gain to 10.

drills.prompt: What does an amplifier give up when negative feedback makes its gain stable and predictable?

choices.text: Gain: the closed-loop gain is far below the open-loop gain.
Supply voltage: feedback needs a higher supply.
choices.feedback: Feedback costs no supply voltage. It spends excess gain to buy accuracy, bandwidth and lower distortion.

choices.text: Bandwidth: the closed-loop stage is slower than the open-loop amplifier.
choices.feedback: The other way around. Trading gain for feedback widens the bandwidth: about GBW divided by the noise gain, far beyond the open-loop corner.

glossary.definition: The inverting input of an op amp whose non-inverting input is grounded, held at almost exactly 0 V by negative feedback although nothing connects it to ground. It draws no current itself, so all the current arriving through the input resistor continues through the feedback resistor.

drills.prompt: An inverting amplifier has R_in = 10 kΩ and V_in = 2.0 V. What current flows through R_in?

choices.text: 0 mA, since op-amp inputs draw no current
choices.feedback: The input pin takes none, but R_in does carry current: its far end sits at the virtual ground, 0 V, so (2.0 V − 0 V)/10 kΩ = 0.20 mA flows on into R_f.
The virtual ground fixes R_in's inner end at 0 V whatever R_f is, so the current is 2.0 V / 10 kΩ = 0.20 mA. R_f sets the output instead.

drills.prompt: You probe the inverting input of a working inverting amplifier with an oscilloscope. You see:

choices.text: almost nothing: microvolts to a few millivolts
a copy of the input signal
choices.feedback: Feedback holds that node at the + input's voltage, 0 V; the input signal appears across R_in instead.
The output appears across R_f. The inverting input sits at the virtual ground, about 0 V.

drills.prompt: Why is it called a virtual ground rather than a ground?

choices.text: Its 0 V is held by feedback, not by a connection, and it vanishes if the output saturates.
It connects to ground through a high resistance inside the op amp.
choices.feedback: There is no internal path to ground; the op amp's inputs draw almost no current. The 0 V comes from the output adjusting itself.

choices.text: It is ground for AC signals only.
choices.feedback: It holds 0 V for DC and AC alike, as long as feedback works. It is virtual because no wire makes it so.

glossary.definition: The ratio of a circuit's output signal to its input signal, such as V_out/V_in for voltage gain; a negative gain means the output is inverted. It is often given in decibels, 20·log₁₀ of the voltage ratio.

drills.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has R_f = 47 kΩ and R_g = 4.7 kΩ. What is its voltage gain?

choices.feedback: R_f/R_g = 10 is the inverting stage's gain. A non-inverting stage gives 1 + R_f/R_g = 11, because its output must also lift the − input up to V_in.
That is the inverting configuration. Fed at the + input, the output is in phase: 1 + 47/4.7 = 11.

drills.prompt: What unit does a voltage gain carry?

choices.feedback: A gain compares an output voltage with an input voltage; the volts cancel.
Volts per ampere would be ohms. A voltage gain is volts per volt, a pure number.

drills.prompt: A voltage follower has a voltage gain of 1. Which is true?

choices.text: It can still deliver far more power than the source, from its own supply.

choices.feedback: Its input draws almost nothing while its output can supply tens of milliamps, so it keeps a weak source from being loaded.

choices.text: Its gain in decibels is 1 dB.
choices.feedback: 20·log₁₀(1) = 0 dB. A gain of 1 is 0 dB.

glossary.definition: For an internally compensated op amp, the closed-loop gain times the bandwidth stays about constant, equal to the frequency where the open-loop gain has fallen to 1. A stage with noise gain G therefore has a bandwidth of about GBW/G.

drills.prompt: An op amp with a 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product is used in a non-inverting stage with a gain of 20. About what bandwidth does it have?

choices.feedback: Gain and bandwidth trade, they don't multiply up: bandwidth ≈ GBW/gain = 1 MHz / 20 = 50 kHz.
That is the bandwidth at a gain of 1, as a follower. At a gain of 20 it is 1 MHz / 20 = 50 kHz.

drills.prompt: A design needs a non-inverting gain of 100 with 50 kHz of bandwidth. What gain-bandwidth product must the op amp have, at least?

choices.feedback: That would do only at a gain of 1. Gain × bandwidth = 100 × 50 kHz = 5 MHz.
Dividing instead of multiplying: the product is 100 × 50 kHz = 5 MHz.

drills.prompt: A gain of 100 is needed from op amps with a 1 MHz GBW. Compared with one stage of 100, two stages of 10 in cascade give:

choices.text: much more bandwidth: about 64 kHz instead of 10 kHz
the same bandwidth, because the GBW is fixed
choices.feedback: The GBW is per op amp, and two stages use two. Each stage of 10 reaches 100 kHz; together about 64 kHz, against 10 kHz for one stage of 100.

choices.text: less bandwidth, because each stage adds its own roll-off
choices.feedback: Each stage does roll off, but at 100 kHz instead of 10 kHz; the pair is down 3 dB at about 64 kHz, still far above 10 kHz.

drills.prompt: Does the bandwidth set by the GBW depend on the signal's amplitude?

choices.text: No: it is a small-signal limit; the slew rate is the limit that depends on amplitude.
Yes: larger signals get less bandwidth.
choices.feedback: That describes slew-rate limiting, a separate effect. The GBW limit applies the same way to any small signal.

choices.text: Yes: larger signals get more bandwidth.
choices.feedback: Amplitude doesn't widen any op-amp limit. The GBW limit is the same for any small signal; slew rate cuts large ones further.

glossary.definition: The fastest rate at which an amplifier's output voltage can change, usually given in V/µs. A sine of peak V_p and frequency f needs a slope of 2πf·V_p at its zero crossings, and when that exceeds the slew rate it is distorted toward a triangle.

drills.prompt: Which unit is a slew rate given in?

choices.feedback: Frequency enters through the sine's slope, but the slew rate itself is a rate of change of voltage: volts per microsecond.
Volts per volt is a gain. A slew rate is volts per unit time.
A time alone is a rise time. The slew rate is how many volts the output moves per microsecond.

drills.prompt: An op amp slews at 0.5 V/µs and must deliver a sine of 10 V peak. About what is the highest clean frequency?

choices.feedback: 0.5 V/µs divided by 10 V is 50 000 per second, but a sine's steepest slope is 2πf·V_p, not f·V_p: divide by 2π, about 8.0 kHz.
That uses the 20 V peak-to-peak swing. The steepest slope is 2πf·V_p with the peak, 10 V: f = 500 000 V/s / (2π × 10 V) ≈ 8.0 kHz.

drills.prompt: A sine is slew limited at the output. You halve its amplitude at the same frequency. What happens?

choices.text: It may come out clean: the slope it needs has halved.
Nothing changes: bandwidth limits don't depend on amplitude.
choices.feedback: That holds for the GBW limit. The slew rate limits slope, 2πf·V_p, which halves with the amplitude.
A smaller swing needs a smaller slope, 2πf·V_p, so the output is less likely to hit the slew limit.

glossary.definition: A circuit, often an op amp with no negative feedback or a dedicated comparator chip, whose output switches to one of two levels depending on which input is higher. It turns an analog voltage into a logic decision at a threshold.

drills.prompt: A comparator powered from 0 V and 5 V has 2.5 V from a divider on its + input and a sensor on its − input. The sensor reads 3.1 V. The output is:

choices.feedback: The output goes high when V+ is above V−. Here the sensor on the − input is higher, so the output goes low.
With no feedback the output doesn't follow the input; it goes to one level or the other. V− > V+ sends it low.

drills.prompt: Which is true of an op amp used as a comparator?

choices.text: Its inputs can sit far apart: the equal-inputs rule needs negative feedback.
Its inputs are held equal, as in an amplifier.
choices.feedback: Only negative feedback holds them equal. Without it, they sit wherever the circuit puts them, and the output reports which is higher.

choices.text: Its output is proportional to the input difference.
choices.feedback: Only within microvolts of the switching point. Beyond that the huge open-loop gain sends the output to a rail.

drills.prompt: A comparator's reference comes from a divider across 5.0 V: 30 kΩ on top, 20 kΩ to ground. At what input voltage does it switch?

choices.feedback: That is the drop across the top resistor. The reference is across the bottom one: 5.0 V × 20/(30 + 20) = 2.0 V.
5.0 × 20/30 uses the ratio of the two resistors. The divider fraction is R2 over the total: 20/50, so 2.0 V.

glossary.definition: A difference between the input level that switches a circuit one way and the level that switches it back. In a Schmitt trigger, positive feedback creates the two thresholds, so noise smaller than the gap between them can't make the output chatter.

drills.prompt: Why doesn't a Schmitt trigger chatter on a slow, noisy input?

choices.text: Once it switches, its threshold jumps away from the input, so noise must cross the whole gap to switch it back.
A capacitor inside it filters the noise out.
choices.feedback: No capacitor is needed. The two thresholds, made by positive feedback, do the work.

choices.text: Its output switches more slowly than a comparator's.
choices.feedback: It switches just as fast; it switches once, because the second threshold is out of the noise's reach.

drills.prompt: A Schmitt trigger switches high when its input rises past 2.6 V and low when it falls past 2.4 V. The input carries 50 mV peak-to-peak of noise. Does it chatter at a crossing?

choices.text: No: the 0.2 V gap is wider than the noise
Yes: any noise near a threshold causes chatter
choices.feedback: That is true for a plain comparator, with one threshold. Here the input must fall 0.2 V to switch back, and 50 mV of noise can't do that.

choices.text: Only if the noise exceeds 2.4 V
choices.feedback: What matters is the gap between the thresholds, 2.6 − 2.4 = 0.2 V, against the 50 mV of noise. The gap wins, so no chatter.

drills.prompt: Which connection gives a comparator hysteresis?

choices.text: Positive feedback: a resistor from the output to the + input
Negative feedback: a resistor from the output to the − input
choices.feedback: That makes a linear amplifier; the output no longer snaps between two levels.

choices.text: A capacitor between the two inputs
choices.feedback: That only slows the input. Hysteresis needs the output to move the threshold, through positive feedback.

glossary.definition: A two-terminal part, usually a PN junction, that conducts readily when its anode is more positive than its cathode and blocks current the other way. A conducting silicon diode drops about 0.6–0.7 V over a wide range of current.

drills.prompt: Which way does a diode conduct, judged from its symbol?

choices.text: Along the triangle's point, from anode to cathode, toward the bar
Toward the triangle's flat side, from cathode to anode
choices.feedback: The triangle points the way conventional current flows: anode to cathode. The bar marks the cathode.

choices.text: Either way, depending on the voltage
choices.feedback: In normal use it conducts only from anode to cathode; reverse current flows only in breakdown, which a Zener uses on purpose.

drills.prompt: A silicon diode in series with 1.0 kΩ is forward biased by a 5.0 V supply. About what current flows?

choices.feedback: That ignores the diode's drop. About 0.7 V stays across the diode, so the resistor gets 4.3 V: 4.3 mA.
That puts the diode's 0.7 V across the resistor. The resistor takes the rest, 5.0 − 0.7 = 4.3 V.

drills.prompt: The same diode is turned around in that 5 V circuit. The current is:

choices.text: almost none: nanoamps to microamps of leakage

choices.feedback: Reversed, the junction blocks. Only a tiny leakage flows until breakdown, which for a rectifier or small-signal diode is tens of volts or more.

choices.text: large, because the diode breaks down
choices.feedback: 5 V is far below a typical diode's breakdown voltage, tens of volts or more. It simply blocks.

glossary.definition: The voltage across a conducting diode from anode to cathode: about 0.6–0.7 V for a silicon junction, 0.2–0.4 V for a Schottky, and about 1.2 V (infrared) to 3.3 V (blue) for an LED, rising with the photon energy. It rises only about 60–120 mV for each tenfold increase in current, which is why a diode is often modeled as a fixed drop.

drills.prompt: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2.0 V runs from 5.0 V at 10 mA. What series resistor does it need?

choices.feedback: 5.0 V / 10 mA ignores the LED. The resistor only gets what the LED leaves: (5.0 − 2.0) V / 10 mA = 300 Ω.
2.0 V / 10 mA uses the LED's voltage. The resistor takes the other 3.0 V: 300 Ω.

drills.prompt: A silicon diode carries a fixed current and warms up. Its forward voltage:

choices.feedback: At a fixed current the drop falls as the junction warms, about 2 mV per °C; that is how a diode works as a temperature sensor.
0.7 V is a model. The real drop falls about 2 mV per °C, and it also shifts with current.

drills.prompt: At the same current, which has the lowest forward voltage?

choices.feedback: A silicon junction drops about 0.6–0.7 V; a Schottky's metal–semiconductor junction drops about 0.2–0.4 V.
A blue LED drops about 3 V: its wide band gap, which sets the photon energy, also sets a high forward voltage.

glossary.definition: A diode made to break down at a specified reverse voltage V_Z, so it can conduct in reverse with its voltage held nearly constant over a wide range of current. With a series resistor to set its current, it makes a simple voltage reference or regulator.

drills.prompt: A 5.1 V Zener diode is fed from 12 V through 680 Ω, with no load. About what current does it carry?

choices.feedback: 12 V / 680 Ω forgets the Zener's voltage. The resistor gets only 12 − 5.1 = 6.9 V: about 10 mA.
5.1 V / 680 Ω uses the Zener's voltage. The resistor takes the difference, 6.9 V: about 10 mA.

drills.prompt: Which is true of a Zener regulator with a series resistor?

choices.text: The Zener takes whatever current the load doesn't, so it dissipates most with no load.
The Zener's current stays constant as the load changes.
choices.feedback: The resistor's current is nearly constant, set by (V_in − V_Z)/R. The load and the Zener share it, so the Zener's current falls as the load draws more.

choices.text: It works without the series resistor.
choices.feedback: The Zener's voltage barely moves with current, so a stiff supply across it alone would drive a destructive current. The resistor sets the current.

drills.prompt: A 5.1 V Zener diode is wired in forward. About what does it drop?

choices.feedback: V_Z applies only in reverse breakdown. Forward, it is an ordinary PN junction.
Forward, it still has a junction to cross: about 0.7 V, like any silicon diode.

glossary.definition: A light-emitting diode: a PN junction in a direct-band-gap semiconductor that emits light when electrons and holes recombine. Its forward voltage rises with the photon energy, from about 1.8 V for red to about 3 V for blue and white.

drills.prompt: Why does an LED on a voltage supply need a series resistor or a current driver?

choices.text: Its current rises steeply with its voltage, so something else must set the current.
Its forward voltage is too high otherwise.
choices.feedback: Its forward voltage is set by its band gap; nothing lowers it. The problem is that a small change in voltage changes the current a lot.

choices.text: To protect it against reverse voltage.
choices.feedback: Reverse protection is a separate matter. The series resistor sets the forward current.

drills.prompt: Two white LEDs with a forward voltage of 3.0 V each run in series from 9.0 V at 20 mA. What series resistor do they need?

choices.feedback: That allows for only one LED: (9.0 − 3.0) V / 20 mA. Both drop 3.0 V, leaving 3.0 V for the resistor: 150 Ω.
9.0 V / 20 mA ignores both LEDs. They take 6.0 V, leaving 3.0 V: 150 Ω.

drills.prompt: At the same current, which LED has the highest forward voltage?

choices.feedback: Red photons carry the least energy of the visible colors, so a red LED drops the least, about 1.8–2 V.
Infrared photons carry less energy than visible light, so an IR LED drops even less than red, about 1.2–1.5 V.

glossary.definition: A bipolar junction transistor: three layers, NPN or PNP, in which a small base current controls a collector current about β times larger. Its base–emitter junction is a diode, so a conducting silicon BJT has about 0.6–0.7 V from base to emitter.

drills.prompt: An NPN transistor switches a load from 12 V. Where does the load go?

choices.text: Between 12 V and the collector, with the emitter grounded
Between the emitter and ground, with the collector on 12 V
choices.feedback: That makes an emitter follower: the emitter sits about 0.7 V below the base, so the load gets at most the drive voltage less 0.7 V, never the full 12 V. A switch puts the load in the collector.
The base carries only the small control current. The load current flows from collector to emitter.

drills.prompt: An NPN with β = 100 is in its active region with a base current of 20 µA. What is the collector current?

choices.feedback: That is the base current. In the active region the collector carries β times it: 100 × 20 µA = 2.0 mA.
100 × 20 µA = 2000 µA = 2.0 mA. Check the prefixes.

drills.prompt: In a BJT's active region, its junctions are:

choices.text: base–emitter forward biased, base–collector reverse biased

choices.feedback: That is saturation, where the transistor acts like a closed switch.
That is cutoff, where no collector current flows.

glossary.definition: A BJT's current gain, the ratio of collector current to base current in the active region (h_FE on datasheets), typically 50 to 300 and varying widely between parts and with temperature. A switch is driven with a forced β, I_C/I_B, of about 10, so every part saturates.

drills.prompt: An NPN switch must carry 100 mA. With a forced β of 10, what base current do you supply?

choices.feedback: A part with β = 100 would sit just at the edge of saturation, and any lower-β part wouldn't saturate. A forced β of 10 leaves margin: 100 mA / 10 = 10 mA.
The base current is the collector current divided by the forced β, 100 mA / 10 = 10 mA, not multiplied by it.

drills.prompt: Which is true of β?

choices.text: It can differ by a factor of three or more between parts of the same type.
It is fixed for each part number.
choices.feedback: Datasheets give a wide range, often 100 to 300 for one part number, and it shifts with current and temperature. Good designs work over the whole range.

choices.text: It is the voltage gain of a common-emitter stage.
choices.feedback: β is a current ratio. A common-emitter stage's voltage gain is set by its resistors, about −R_C/R_E.

drills.prompt: A bias circuit gives I_C = 1.0 mA with a β = 100 part. Swapped for a β = 300 part, the collector current triples. Which bias did it use?

choices.text: A single resistor from the supply to the base, which fixes the base current
A stiff divider on the base with an emitter resistor
choices.feedback: That fixes the base voltage, so the emitter current is about (V_B − 0.7 V)/R_E whatever β is. Swapping parts would barely change I_C.

choices.text: A current source in the emitter
choices.feedback: An emitter current source fixes I_E directly; I_C ≈ I_E for any large β, so it wouldn't triple.

glossary.definition: The state in which more drive no longer raises the output: a saturated BJT has both junctions forward biased and only about 0.2 V from collector to emitter, an op amp's output stops near a supply rail, and an inductor's core can magnetize no further, so its inductance falls sharply. For a MOSFET the same word names the region in which the drain current stops rising with V_DS, the counterpart of a BJT's active region, not its saturation.

drills.prompt: An NPN switch with β = 100 gets 5.0 mA of base current and drives a 220 Ω load from 9.0 V, with V_CE(sat) = 0.2 V. What is the collector current?

choices.feedback: β·I_B = 100 × 5.0 mA is what the base could support, but the load allows only (9.0 − 0.2) V / 220 Ω = 40 mA. With the base overdriven the transistor saturates, and the supply and the load set the current.
That is the base current. The collector carries the load current, set in saturation by the supply and the load: (9.0 − 0.2) V / 220 Ω = 40 mA.

drills.prompt: A BJT switch should be on, but its collector reads 4 V on a 12 V supply with the load connected. What is wrong?

choices.text: It isn't saturated: too little base current leaves it in the active region, hot.
Nothing: 4 V is a normal saturation voltage.
choices.feedback: V_CE(sat) is about 0.2 V. At 4 V the transistor is in its active region, limited by β·I_B, and dissipating 4 V times the collector current.
Off, no current flows, so the load drops nothing and the collector sits at the full 12 V. At 4 V current is flowing; there just isn't enough base drive.

drills.prompt: A MOSFET in a current driver is said to be "in saturation", and so is a BJT in a switch. Which is true?

choices.text: The MOSFET is in its constant-current region; the BJT is fully on, like a closed switch.
Both are fully on, with little voltage across them.
choices.feedback: That is the BJT meaning. A MOSFET that is fully on, acting as a resistor, is in its triode region; its saturation region is where the current levels off and V_DS can be large.

choices.text: Both are in their constant-current region.
choices.feedback: That is the MOSFET meaning. A BJT's constant-current region is the active region; a saturated BJT has only about 0.2 V across it.

drills.prompt: An inductor runs above its rated saturation current. What happens?

choices.text: Its inductance drops sharply, so the current rises much faster than expected.
Its inductance rises, smoothing the current more.
choices.feedback: A saturated core can carry no more flux, so its permeability, and with it the inductance, falls.
Heating is set by the RMS current and the winding resistance. Saturation is a separate, magnetic limit: the inductance falls as soon as the peak current passes it.

glossary.definition: A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: the gate voltage, insulated from the channel by a thin oxide, controls the current from drain to source. The gate draws no steady current, only a brief current to charge or discharge its capacitance at each switching edge.

drills.prompt: What controls an N-channel MOSFET's drain current?

choices.text: The gate current, as a base current controls a BJT
choices.feedback: The gate is insulated by oxide, so it draws essentially no steady current. The voltage on it controls the channel.
The channel forms with respect to the source: V_GS sets it. V_DS then decides between the triode and saturation regions.

drills.prompt: A microcontroller pin switches a MOSFET at 20 kHz. Which is true of the pin's current?

choices.text: Brief pulses at each edge to charge and discharge the gate, and none in between
None at all, since the gate is insulated
choices.feedback: No steady current, but the gate is a capacitor, often nanofarads: each edge must move its gate charge Q_g.

choices.text: A steady current of I_D divided by the transistor's gain
choices.feedback: That is how a BJT's base works. A MOSFET's gate draws current only while its voltage changes.

drills.prompt: A MOSFET's gate is left unconnected. Which is true?

choices.text: It may sit partly on: charge stranded on the gate capacitance holds a voltage, so a pull-down resistor is needed.
It turns off, since no gate current flows.
choices.feedback: With no path to discharge it, the gate keeps whatever charge it picked up, and stray fields can add more. A pull-down resistor holds it off.

choices.text: It conducts fully, as an open gate reads as high.
choices.feedback: Its state is undefined, not high: anything from off to partly on, which can overheat it. A pull-down resistor fixes the state.

glossary.definition: The gate-to-source voltage V_t at which a MOSFET's channel just forms and drain current begins to flow, often 1–4 V for power parts. At its threshold a MOSFET is barely on; full conduction needs the higher V_GS at which its datasheet specifies R_DS(on).

drills.prompt: A MOSFET's datasheet gives a gate threshold of 2–4 V and specifies R_DS(on) at V_GS = 10 V. Can a 3.3 V logic pin switch it fully on?

choices.text: No: 3.3 V lies inside the 2–4 V threshold range, where the channel barely conducts, if at all.

choices.feedback: At threshold a MOSFET only starts to conduct, and a part can have a threshold up to 4 V. Full conduction needs V_GS near the 10 V its R_DS(on) is specified at, or a logic-level part.

choices.text: Yes: any gate voltage above 0 V turns it fully on.
choices.feedback: Below threshold there is no channel at all; just above it, a weak one. The datasheet's R_DS(on) needs 10 V here.

drills.prompt: An NMOS has V_t = 1.5 V and K = 2 mA/V², and is in saturation with V_GS = 2.5 V. What is its drain current, I_D = K(V_GS − V_t)²?

choices.feedback: That squares V_GS itself: 2 × 2.5². Only the overdrive above threshold counts: V_GS − V_t = 1.0 V, so 2 × 1.0² = 2.0 mA.
That squares the threshold, 2 × 1.5². The current depends on the overdrive above it: 2 mA/V² × (2.5 V − 1.5 V)² = 2.0 mA.

drills.prompt: A MOSFET warms up. Its threshold voltage:

choices.text: falls, by a few millivolts per °C
rises, so it switches off when hot
choices.feedback: The threshold falls with temperature. At a fixed gate voltage near threshold, a warm MOSFET conducts more, not less.

choices.text: stays fixed: it is set by the oxide thickness
choices.feedback: The oxide matters, but the threshold also depends on temperature: it falls a few millivolts per °C.

glossary.definition: The resistance R_DS(on) from drain to source of a MOSFET driven fully on: milliohms for power parts, ohms for small-signal ones. It is specified at a stated gate voltage and rises with temperature, often by 1.5 to 2 times between 25 °C and 125 °C.

drills.prompt: A fully on MOSFET with R_DS(on) = 50 mΩ carries 4.0 A. What does it dissipate?

choices.feedback: 4.0 A × 50 mΩ = 0.20 V is the voltage across it. The power is I²·R = 4.0² × 0.050 = 0.80 W.

drills.prompt: Why does a MOSFET switch's conduction loss quadruple when its current doubles?

choices.text: P = I²·R_DS(on): the voltage across it doubles along with the current.

choices.feedback: At a given gate voltage and temperature it is roughly constant. The square comes from P = I·(I·R).
The voltage across the switch, I·R_DS(on), also doubles, so the power I²·R_DS(on) goes up four times.

drills.prompt: What gate drive does a MOSFET need for its datasheet R_DS(on)?

choices.text: At least the V_GS stated with the R_DS(on) figure, such as 4.5 V or 10 V
Anything just above the threshold voltage
choices.feedback: Just above threshold the channel is weak and the resistance high. R_DS(on) is guaranteed only at the stated V_GS.

choices.text: Any gate voltage: R_DS(on) is fixed
choices.feedback: The channel resistance falls as V_GS rises; the datasheet figure holds only at the V_GS it states.

glossary.definition: A circuit of diodes that turns AC into DC of one polarity: a half-wave rectifier passes one half of each cycle, and a full-wave bridge flips the other half up as well. Its output pulses, so a reservoir capacitor usually follows to hold it near the peak.

drills.prompt: A transformer winding of 12 V RMS feeds a silicon bridge rectifier and a large reservoir capacitor. About what is the DC output at light load?

choices.feedback: 12 V RMS is the heating value. The capacitor charges to the peak, √2 × 12 ≈ 17.0 V, less two diode drops.
That subtracts one diode drop. In a bridge two diodes conduct in series on each half-cycle: 17.0 − 1.4 ≈ 15.6 V.
That is the winding's peak. The two conducting diodes drop about 1.4 V: 15.6 V.

drills.prompt: With the same capacitor and load, why does a full-wave rectifier give half the ripple of a half-wave one?

choices.text: It refills the capacitor twice per cycle, so the capacitor discharges for half as long.
Its output voltage is twice as high.
choices.feedback: The peak is the same, less one more diode drop. The ripple halves because the gap between refills halves.

choices.text: It has more diodes, which filter the output.
choices.feedback: Diodes don't filter. The capacitor does, and it has half as long to sag between refills.

drills.prompt: In a rectifier feeding a reservoir capacitor, the current through the diodes is:

choices.text: short pulses near each peak, much larger than the load current
a steady current equal to the load current
choices.feedback: The diodes conduct only while the input is above the capacitor's voltage, a short part of each cycle. All the charge the load used must go back in then, so the pulses are large.

choices.text: a sine wave in phase with the input
choices.feedback: The diodes are reverse biased for most of the cycle, while the capacitor holds the output above the input.

glossary.definition: The periodic variation left on a DC voltage or current after rectification or switching, usually given peak to peak. With a reservoir capacitor it is about I/(f·C) for a half-wave rectifier and half that for full-wave; a switching converter's ripple is at its switching frequency.

drills.prompt: A full-wave rectifier on the 60 Hz line feeds 0.50 A from a 2200 µF reservoir capacitor. About what is the peak-to-peak ripple?

choices.feedback: I/(f·C) is the half-wave figure. A bridge refills at 120 Hz, twice per cycle, which halves it: 0.50 / (120 × 0.0022) ≈ 1.9 V.
2200 µF is 2.2 × 10⁻³ F. Then 0.50 / (2 × 60 × 0.0022) ≈ 1.9 V, not millivolts.

drills.prompt: The load current on a capacitor-input rectifier doubles. The ripple:

choices.feedback: More current drains the capacitor faster between peaks: ΔV ≈ I/(2f·C) for full-wave rises with I.

choices.text: stays the same, set by the capacitor and the frequency
choices.feedback: The capacitor loses charge I·Δt between peaks, so ΔV ≈ I/(2f·C) is proportional to the load current.

drills.prompt: Which change reduces a buck converter's inductor ripple current, with the same inductor and the same input and output voltages?

choices.feedback: Each on-time would be longer, so the current ramps further: ΔI = (V_in − V_out)·D/(f·L) grows as f falls.
In continuous conduction the load sets the average inductor current, not its ripple. ΔI = (V_in − V_out)·D/(f·L) has no load term.

glossary.definition: Pulse-width modulation: switching a load fully on and fully off at a fixed frequency and varying the fraction of each period it is on, the duty cycle. The load, or a filter after the switch, responds to the average, D times the full voltage, while the switch wastes little power because it is never half on.

drills.prompt: A 12 V supply drives a motor through a MOSFET switched by PWM at a 25 % duty cycle. Ignoring the drops in the switch and the flyback diode, what average voltage does the motor see?

choices.feedback: The motor sees 12 V only while the switch is on, a quarter of the time, and about 0 V otherwise: the average is 0.25 × 12 V = 3.0 V.
That is the off fraction, 75 %, of 12 V. The switch is on for 25 %: 3.0 V.

drills.prompt: Why does PWM dim a lamp more efficiently than a series resistor?

choices.text: The switch is either fully on, with little voltage across it, or off, with no current, so it dissipates little.

choices.feedback: The supply stays the same; the switch connects it for only part of each period. The saving comes from the switch never being half on.
The lamp is unchanged. A series resistor burns power whenever current flows; a switch that is fully on or off burns almost none.

drills.prompt: An LED is driven by PWM at 1 kHz with a 50 % duty cycle. What does the eye see?

choices.text: Steady light, with half the average light output of full on

choices.feedback: The eye can't follow 1 kHz. It averages the pulses into steady light.

choices.text: Full brightness, since the LED is fully on when it is on
choices.feedback: The LED is fully on half the time and off the rest; the eye integrates that into half the average output.

glossary.definition: The fraction D of each switching period during which a switch is on, from 0 to 1 or 0 to 100 %. In an ideal buck converter the output voltage is D times the input.

drills.prompt: A switch is on for 3.0 µs of every 10 µs. What are its duty cycle and switching frequency?

choices.feedback: The switching frequency is 1/period = 1/(10 µs) = 100 kHz. 1/(3.0 µs) is the reciprocal of the on-time.
3/7 compares the on-time with the off-time. The duty cycle is the on-time over the whole period: 3.0/10 = 0.30.

drills.prompt: An ideal buck converter makes 3.3 V from 12 V. What duty cycle does it run at?

choices.feedback: That is the off fraction, 1 − D. A buck gives V_out = D·V_in, so D = 3.3/12 ≈ 0.28.
12/3.3 is upside down, and a duty cycle can't exceed 1: D = V_out/V_in = 3.3/12 ≈ 0.28.

drills.prompt: In what unit is a duty cycle given?

choices.feedback: The on-time is in seconds; the duty cycle is the on-time divided by the period, so the seconds cancel.
Hertz measures the switching frequency. The duty cycle is a fraction of each period.

glossary.definition: A switching converter that steps a DC voltage down: a switch chops the input, and an inductor and capacitor pass on its average, so V_out = D·V_in. It wastes little power, so it draws less current from its input than it delivers to its load.

drills.prompt: An ideal buck converter makes 5.0 V at 2.0 A from 20 V. What current does it draw from the 20 V supply?

choices.feedback: That is what a linear regulator would draw: the same current in as out. A buck trades voltage for current: 10 W in at 20 V is 0.50 A.
Power in equals power out, so the higher voltage means less current, not more: 10 W / 20 V = 0.50 A.

drills.prompt: Why can a buck converter be far more efficient than a linear regulator?

choices.text: Its switch is never half on, and the inductor stores energy rather than burning the difference.
It drops the voltage across a smaller resistor.
choices.feedback: There is no dropping resistor. The switch is fully on or fully off, and the inductor and capacitor average the chopped voltage.
It uses more: a switch, an inductor, a capacitor and a controller. Its efficiency comes from never dissipating the voltage difference.

drills.prompt: Why does a buck converter's average inductor current equal its load current?

choices.text: The output capacitor passes no steady current, so on average all the inductor's current goes to the load.
The inductor regulates its own current to match the load.
choices.feedback: An inductor doesn't regulate anything; it carries whatever its voltage builds up. The capacitor can't take a steady current, so the average must go to the load.

choices.text: The switch carries the load current all the time.
choices.feedback: The switch conducts only during the on-time, so its average current is D times the load current. The inductor carries current all period.

glossary.definition: A diode across an inductive load such as a relay coil or a motor, reverse biased in normal operation, that gives the coil's current a path when the switch opens. Without it the current would be forced to stop at once, and the kickback L·di/dt could reach hundreds of volts and destroy the switch.

drills.prompt: An NPN low-side switch drives a 12 V relay coil. Where does the flyback diode go?

choices.text: Across the coil, cathode to the 12 V end
Across the coil, anode to the 12 V end
choices.feedback: Then it is forward biased whenever the switch is on and short-circuits the supply through the transistor.
In series it can only block current. The coil's current needs a loop that bypasses the opened switch: a diode across the coil.

drills.prompt: A 100 mH coil carries 50 mA. With no flyback diode, the switch forces the current to zero in 1 µs. About what voltage would the coil produce?

choices.feedback: That would be a fall over 1 ms. Over 1 µs, v = L·di/dt = 0.1 H × 0.05 A / 10⁻⁶ s = 5000 V: the short time is what makes it huge.
0.1 H × 0.05 A = 0.005 Wb is the coil's flux linkage, not a voltage. The voltage is how fast it changes: divide by 1 µs, v = L·di/dt = 5000 V.

drills.prompt: A plain flyback diode makes a relay release a little later. Why?

choices.text: The coil's current circulates through the diode and decays slowly, opposed only by about 0.7 V and the coil's resistance.
The diode stores charge that holds the relay closed.
choices.feedback: A diode stores very little charge. The delay comes from the coil's current circulating through the diode, decaying at a rate set by L and its small loop voltage.

choices.text: It doesn't; the relay releases at the same moment.
choices.feedback: The coil's current, and so its magnetic pull, now dies away over a time of about L/R instead of at once, so the release comes later.
